column3: Calibration Drift in Low-Cost Particulate Matter Sensors
Journal of Urban Sensing, vol. 12 (2026)
Calibration Drift in Low-Cost Particulate Matter Sensors Deployed Across an Urban Monitoring Network
I. Vandersloot1, T. Achterberg1 and P. Nandakumar2
1Institute for Urban Sensing, Northvale University · 2Department of Atmospheric Science, Eastmere Technical College
Abstract

Low-cost optical sensors have made dense air-quality monitoring affordable, but their readings drift as the instruments age. We followed 84 sensors for eighteen months beside three reference monitors and modelled the drift as a slow linear trend plus a humidity-dependent term. Median drift reached 2.1 µg/m³ per month in the wet season, and a monthly recalibration against a single nearby reference removed 78 percent of the accumulated error. We recommend scheduled recalibration instead of fixed replacement cycles.
Keywords: air quality, particulate matter, sensor drift, calibration
1 Introduction

Cities increasingly rely on networks of inexpensive particulate matter sensors to map exposure at the scale of a single street. A unit costs less than one hundredth of a reference monitor, which allows a network to cover entire districts. The price comes with a limitation: the optical chamber of each unit gradually collects dust, and the response of the photodiode changes with temperature and humidity. Earlier studies reported drift over periods of a few weeks. Little is known about the behaviour over a full year, which is the horizon on which municipal networks are planned and budgeted. This paper addresses that gap with an eighteen-month field comparison. The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 describes the network and the model, Section 3 reports the results, and Section 4 discusses their implications for network operators. Our contributions are the following:
(i) a public data set of 84 co-located sensors;
(ii) a drift model with an explicit humidity term;
(iii) a recalibration policy evaluated on held-out sites.

2.2 Reference instruments
Three sites were equipped with reference-grade monitors operated by the regional agency.2 Hourly means from these monitors served as the ground truth for all comparisons.
2.3 Drift model
For each unit the deviation d(t) from the nearest reference was modelled as
d(t) = a + b·t + c·h(t) + ε(t)
where t is the time since installation, h(t) the relative humidity and ε(t) a noise term with variance σ². We fitted the coefficients by ordinary least squares and report b as the drift rate.
2.4 Data processing

Readings were aggregated to hourly means before analysis. Hours with fewer than forty-five valid readings were discarded, which removed 3.2 percent of the data. Outliers beyond five median absolute deviations were flagged and excluded from the fits.

Averaged over all units, recalibration against the nearest reference removed 78 percent of the accumulated error after twelve months. The remaining error was dominated by short-term noise rather than by drift.
4 Discussion

The humidity term explained most of the difference between the dry and the wet season. Units that were fan-forced drifted more slowly, which suggests that airflow reduces the deposition of dust on the optical surfaces. Two limitations should be noted. All sites were located in a temperate climate, and the two sensor models share the same optical principle, so the results may not transfer to other technologies or to very dry regions. Our results have a direct consequence for network operators. A fixed replacement cycle discards units whose readings can still be corrected, whereas scheduled recalibration keeps them in service at a fraction of the cost.

5 Conclusion
We measured calibration drift in 84 low-cost sensors over eighteen months and found a consistent, humidity-dependent
upward
trend.

Scheduled recalibration against a nearby reference is a cheaper and more reliable way to keep low-cost networks usable than replacing units on a fixed cycle. Future work will examine whether a recalibration interval can be chosen automatically from the observed humidity history of each site.

The hourly data of all 84 units and the three reference monitors are available from the project repository under an open licence, together with the scripts used to fit the drift model.
